question.text: An open-plan office in Cambridge, 80 occupants, complaints concentrated in the west-facing zone from 14:00–17:00 during July–August. Building has fixed external louvres set to 60° and a VAV cooling system. The supply air temperature meets setpoint and the VAV box airflow is within its design range. Diagnose the likely overheating issue under CIBSE TM52 methodology and recommend investigation and remediation steps.

answer.text: Likely a combination of solar gain through unshaded portion of west-facing fenestration and inadequate VAV box throw in the west zone. Apply TM52 Criterion 1 (Hours of Exceedance) — modelling will likely show >3% of occupied hours above the upper acceptable limit. Primary cause: fixed louvre angle insufficient for late-afternoon sun azimuth. Secondary causes: VAV box throw distribution may not match the west zone's solar gain profile; cooling capacity may be design-correct but spatially mis-distributed. Recommended steps: (1) dynamic thermal modelling using TM52 against the three criteria; (2) measure surface and air temperatures in the affected zone across a hot week; (3) consider dynamic external blinds or internal blinds for late afternoon; (4) review VAV diffuser layout against zone heat-gain map.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52: The Limits of Thermal Comfort — Avoiding Overheating in European Buildings (2013)

question.text: A top-floor flat in a 1960s tower block, single-aspect south-facing, no mechanical cooling, occupant reports that the bedroom reaches 30°C during summer nights and sleep is impossible. The flat has secondary double-glazing fitted in 2018 and the lounge has trickle vents. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and recommend the most cost-effective remediation.

answer.text: Classic top-floor single-aspect south-facing overheating risk. Apply CIBSE TM59, which is the domestic methodology: TM52 Criterion 1 (hours of exceedance, no more than 3% of occupied hours May–September) for living spaces, plus the TM59 bedroom criterion that operative temperature must not exceed 26°C for more than 1% of annual night hours between 22:00 and 07:00 — about 32 hours. Primary cause: solar gain through unshaded south fenestration combined with stack-driven upward heat accumulation on the top floor. Secondary causes: secondary glazing reduces ventilation effectiveness by limiting opening area; trickle vents are insufficient for night-time purge ventilation; no thermal mass to dampen diurnal swing. Recommended remediation: (1) external solar shading on south windows (most cost-effective single intervention — external blinds or brise-soleil); (2) increase secure night-purge ventilation via grilles or secure window restrictors; (3) consider light-coloured roof finish if landlord cooperation possible; (4) if budget allows, add reflective glazing film to south windows.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013) and TM59 (Domestic Overheating Risk Assessment)

question.text: A school classroom for 30 pupils in Manchester, single-aspect east-facing, with manually operable windows and ceiling-mounted fans. Teachers report stuffy conditions and pupils losing concentration on warm days from 12:00 onwards. The school has CO2 monitoring showing levels routinely above 1500 ppm by mid-afternoon. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and BB101 ventilation guidance.

answer.text: This is a combined thermal comfort and indoor air quality issue typical of legacy single-aspect classrooms. Apply TM52 Criterion 1 plus BB101 (Building Bulletin 101: Ventilation, thermal comfort and indoor air quality in schools 2018) which sets specific limits for educational spaces. Primary cause of stuffiness: inadequate ventilation rate — CO2 above 1500 ppm breaches the BB101 daily-average limit for a naturally ventilated classroom and indicates fresh air supply below the roughly 5 L/s per person that limit corresponds to. Primary cause of thermal discomfort: morning solar gain on east elevation plus internal heat gains (30 occupants + lighting + equipment) accumulating without sufficient purge. Secondary causes: ceiling fans provide air movement but no fresh-air supply; pupils may not open windows due to noise or security concerns; lack of cross-ventilation in single-aspect classroom. Recommended: (1) measure ventilation rate by tracer-gas or CO2-decay test; (2) install or activate hybrid mechanical extract ventilation linked to CO2 sensors; (3) consider external solar shading on east elevation; (4) review window opening policy with teaching staff.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); DfE BB101 (2018)

question.text: An office floor in Leeds, perimeter zones report cold feet and drafts during winter heating season despite zone temperature meeting 21°C setpoint. AHU supply air at 18°C, perimeter fan-coil units (FCUs) provide local heating. The building uses chilled beams over the central zone for cooling. Diagnose the perimeter cold-draught complaint.

answer.text: Classic mixed-mode perimeter cold-draught issue. Apply TM52 with attention to local discomfort indices, particularly the radiant temperature asymmetry (CIBSE Guide A) and draught risk (DR index from BS EN ISO 7730). Primary cause: high downdraught from poorly-performing or single-glazed perimeter glazing combined with low surface temperatures of cold glazing in winter — creating radiant asymmetry exceeding 10 K threshold. Secondary causes: FCU output may be undersized for the perimeter heat loss profile; supply air at 18°C may be entraining at the perimeter and producing localised low temperatures; cold air falls reach ankle level even when bulk zone air at 21°C. Recommended: (1) measure surface temperatures of perimeter glazing in cold weather; (2) measure floor air temperature at ankle height in affected zones; (3) check FCU output against perimeter heat loss calculation; (4) consider perimeter radiant heating or upgrading single-glazed sections to double-glazing; (5) verify AHU supply-air diffuser type and throw against zone layout.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A Section 1.4 (radiant asymmetry); BS EN ISO 7730 (draught risk)

question.text: A hospital ward in Birmingham, north-facing, single-aspect, ward sister reports that on cold winter mornings the patient beds nearest the windows feel uncomfortable to staff and patients despite the ward thermostat reading 22°C. The windows are sealed (no occupant control) and the ward is heated by overhead radiant panels at high level. Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 supplemented by CIBSE Guide A Section 1.4 (radiant temperature asymmetry) and Section A.1 (HTM 03-01 Specialised ventilation for healthcare premises). Primary cause: high radiant temperature asymmetry between the warm ceiling-mounted radiant panels (50–60°C surface) and the cold internal glazing surface (likely 12–14°C in winter), creating discomfort despite bulk air temperature meeting setpoint. CIBSE recommends maximum asymmetry of 5 K for warm ceiling and 10 K for cold wall — both likely exceeded in this configuration. Secondary causes: north-facing single-aspect orientation gives no winter solar gain to mitigate; sealed windows prevent local control; bed positions at perimeter put vulnerable patients in the worst zone. Recommended: (1) measure surface temperatures with infrared thermometer; (2) calculate radiant asymmetry indices; (3) consider supplementing high-level radiant with low-level perimeter heating (panel radiators or trench heating); (4) upgrade glazing if Trust capex permits; (5) review bed-layout policy to keep vulnerable patients away from perimeter in winter.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); Guide A Section 1.4; HTM 03-01

question.text: A residential bedroom in a new-build flat in London, summer 2025. Owner reports that the bedroom reaches 28°C even with mechanical extract ventilation running at boost. Single-aspect west-facing, restrictor-limited windows (100mm max opening due to part of an above-fourth-floor balcony policy), no cooling. Diagnose under TM59 and recommend cost-aware remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM59 (Design methodology for the assessment of overheating risk in homes), which is the appropriate methodology for new-build domestic spaces. TM59 applies the CIBSE TM52 adaptive comfort criteria but with domestic-specific occupancy profiles and the 1% hours-of-exceedance limit for bedrooms during sleeping hours (22:00–07:00). Primary cause: solar gain through west-facing fenestration peaking 14:00–18:00 and persisting into evening with limited ventilation purge capacity due to 100mm window restrictors limiting effective opening area to roughly 5–10% of glazed area. Secondary cause: mechanical extract ventilation provides air change but no cooling; new-build airtightness limits infiltration purge. Recommended cost-aware remediation: (1) external solar shading on west windows — typically £400–800 per window for retrofit external blinds and the single most cost-effective intervention; (2) review window restrictors with building manager — fire/falls safety can be maintained with secure ventilation grilles; (3) consider a portable air conditioning unit as last resort for occupant comfort; (4) light-coloured curtains or reflective film as cheap interim measure.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (Design Methodology for the Assessment of Overheating Risk in Homes, 2017)

question.text: A glass-roofed atrium in a university building in Sheffield, used as a circulation and breakout space. In summer, occupants complain of overheating at upper-level walkways even with ground-floor extract running. In winter, downdraughts complaints from glazed elevations. Diagnose under TM52 and recommend solutions appropriate for a multi-storey atrium space.

answer.text: Classic multi-zone atrium with seasonal opposite-direction problems. Apply TM52 with attention to multi-zone modelling — atrium thermal stratification must be modelled explicitly using CFD or zonal models because mean-air-temperature based assessment is misleading in tall spaces. Summer primary cause: solar gain through roof glazing creating a stratified hot-air layer at upper levels (commonly 5–10 K warmer than ground floor); ground-floor extract pulls cool replacement air at low level but does not address the stack-trapped hot layer. Winter primary cause: cold downdraught from large glazed elevations at low surface temperature (10–12°C) overwhelming the heating supply; this draught descends to ground level and pools. Secondary causes: lack of mid-height intervention (no upper-level extract, no low-level heat curtain). Recommended: (1) CFD or zonal modelling for both summer and winter cases; (2) install upper-level powered extract for summer with night purge sequence; (3) introduce trench heating or radiant heating at the perimeter glazing base for winter; (4) consider switchable or external shading on roof glazing; (5) provide warm-air curtains at building entrances.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE AM10 Natural ventilation in non-domestic buildings

question.text: A care home day room in Norwich, occupied by elderly residents (average age 84) sitting for extended periods. Staff report that residents feel cold in winter even with the heating delivering 23°C air temperature. The room has a tiled floor and a large north-facing single-aspect glazed elevation. Diagnose with attention to the specific comfort needs of older sedentary occupants.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 with specific adjustment for occupant population — elderly sedentary occupants require higher operative temperatures than working-age office occupants, typically 24–26°C compared to standard 21–23°C. Apply CIBSE Guide A operative temperature methodology. Primary cause: standard 23°C air temperature is insufficient for this population; additionally the cold tiled floor produces low ankle temperatures (typically 16–18°C even in heated room) which dominates perceived comfort in seated posture. Mean radiant temperature is also pulled down by the cold north-facing glazing surface. Secondary causes: low metabolic rate of seated elderly occupants (1.0 met or below); thinner skin and reduced thermoregulation in older adults; lack of local heating at floor level. Recommended: (1) measure floor surface and operative temperatures; (2) raise air temperature to 25°C as target; (3) install underfloor heating or warm carpet on the tile floor — the highest-impact intervention; (4) consider perimeter glazing upgrade or thermal blinds for evening use; (5) provide individual blankets for resident comfort variability.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); Guide A Section 1.4 (occupant-specific comfort)

question.text: A retail showroom in Bristol with double-height glazed shopfront. The HVAC system has been re-commissioned after a tenant fit-out but customers complain of cold drafts near the entrance and warm stagnant air at the back of the shop. Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with attention to spatial uniformity of comfort. Primary cause: poor air distribution post-fit-out — likely the diffuser layout was designed for the previous tenant's furniture layout and now mis-aligns with the new layout creating dead zones at the rear and over-throw at the entrance. The double-height glazing creates two compounding issues: a cold downdraught at the entrance from the glazed elevation, and stratification with warm air rising to the back's high ceiling area beyond the occupant zone. Secondary causes: automatic doors causing infiltration spikes during peak retail hours; tenant fit-out may have blocked or redirected supply air paths; HVAC commissioning may not have re-balanced to suit new layout. Recommended: (1) air balance survey of all supply and return diffusers post-fit-out; (2) measure air velocities and temperatures at occupant level on a grid; (3) install warm-air curtain at entrance to mitigate downdraught and infiltration; (4) consider destratification fans for the high-level space; (5) review automatic door scheduling.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Commissioning Code C

question.text: An office building in Edinburgh fitted with a wet-base trench heating system around the perimeter and chilled-water ceiling cassettes in the central zone. Mid-season (April–May) complaints include simultaneous heating and cooling, drafts, and unstable zone temperatures. Diagnose the comfort issue and identify the root mechanical cause.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with attention to control system behaviour. Primary cause: simultaneous heating and cooling — likely a deadband configuration issue in the BMS where heating and cooling overlap rather than have a sufficient deadband (typically 2–3 K) between heating setpoint and cooling setpoint. This is most pronounced in mid-season when external temperatures swing across the deadband within a single occupied period. Secondary causes: the perimeter trench heating responds slowly (high thermal mass of the wet system) while the chilled ceiling cassettes respond quickly, creating control loop interactions; perimeter solar gain (Edinburgh April is sunny with cold air) drives cooling demand at the perimeter even when heating is technically active. Recommended: (1) review BMS heating and cooling setpoints to ensure proper deadband (e.g. heat to 21°C, cool above 24°C); (2) implement seasonal change-over or sequence-of-operation logic to prevent simultaneous operation; (3) investigate use of a mid-season free-cooling mode using AHU economiser; (4) measure surface temperatures and trace BMS valve positions over a typical mid-season day.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide H — Building Control Systems

question.text: An open-plan office in central London, fully glazed (3 sides), 6th floor with no neighbouring buildings shading it. Occupants on the south and west sides report afternoon overheating despite the active chilled beam system being at full capacity. The cooling plant is sized correctly per design calculations. Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with consideration that chilled beams have inherent capacity limits per unit floor area. Primary cause: solar gain on south and west elevations significantly exceeds the design assumptions used for chilled beam sizing — typical chilled beam capacity is 30–60 W/m² total cooling, of which sensible cooling is dominant. South and west fully-glazed elevations at peak solar can deliver 200–400 W/m² of solar gain, overwhelming the beam capacity even when the plant is at full output. Secondary causes: chilled beams provide convective cooling not radiant — they cannot directly counter the radiant load from hot glass surfaces (mean radiant temperature elevated); occupant complaints aggregate the local discomfort even at meeting design air temperature setpoint. Recommended: (1) measure mean radiant temperature in worst-affected zones — likely 3–5 K above air temperature; (2) calculate operative temperature; (3) review solar gain calculations against actual fenestration g-value and shading; (4) the structural fix is external solar shading or switchable glazing — the design did not account for actual envelope; (5) interim: consider booster fan-coil units in worst-affected areas; (6) consider tinted internal blinds during peak hours.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide B2 (chilled beam systems)

question.text: A university library reading room in Cambridge, 4-metre ceiling, large north-facing windows for daylight, mixed-mode ventilation with displacement supply at low level. Occupants complain of cold feet and lower-leg coolness even in mid-season. The supply air temperature meets setpoint at 18°C. Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with attention to displacement ventilation specifics. Primary cause: displacement ventilation by design produces a vertical temperature gradient with cooler air at floor level (typically 18–19°C) and warmer air at head height (21–23°C) — the discomfort is intrinsic to the system. The complaint is the displacement system functioning as designed. Secondary causes: north-facing glazing produces low surface temperatures contributing to cold radiation onto ankles; supply at 18°C is at the cold end of recommended displacement supply range (some practitioners recommend 19–20°C for sedentary occupants); thin floor finishes amplify ankle coolness. Recommended: (1) measure vertical temperature gradient in occupied zones — CIBSE Guide A and ISO 7730 set a 3 K limit between head and ankle; (2) raise supply air temperature to 19–20°C if gradient is too steep; (3) reduce supply diffuser velocity to limit floor cooling jet; (4) consider supplementary radiant heating along the north-facing perimeter; (5) recommend appropriate occupant footwear if cultural context allows.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide B2 (displacement ventilation); ISO 7730 vertical gradient

question.text: A residential block in Birmingham, 1960s tower block, undergone full retrofit including external wall insulation, triple-glazing replacement, and mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR). Post-retrofit, residents report stuffy and warm conditions year-round, with some bedrooms exceeding 27°C even in mild weather. Diagnose this post-retrofit issue.

answer.text: Classic post-retrofit overheating — apply TM59 (Domestic overheating) supplemented by AECB or Passivhaus retrofit guidance. Primary cause: the retrofit has dramatically reduced fabric heat loss while internal gains (occupants, appliances, lighting, cooking, hot water) remained constant. Without active cooling or summer bypass strategy, the building cannot reject the internal heat gains during warmer periods. The MVHR may not have summer bypass enabled, or the bypass may be functioning but cannot purge the building when external is warmer than internal. Secondary causes: triple glazing reduces effective opening area for purge ventilation; the airtightness post-retrofit means infiltration is now insufficient to cool the building overnight; MVHR design rates (around 0.5 ach) are insufficient for summer cooling. Recommended: (1) check MVHR has summer bypass mode and verify it is operating; (2) measure airtightness and infiltration rate; (3) install or enable purge ventilation strategy — secure night-time window opening; (4) consider light-coloured external finishes for summer solar load; (5) review whether shading was incorporated in the retrofit; (6) educate occupants on summer behaviour (closing curtains during the day, opening windows at night).
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); AECB Retrofit guidance; PHPP overheating analysis

question.text: A coworking space in Manchester, occupied by 60–80 hot-desking workers, fitted with active chilled beam cooling and modern LED lighting. End-of-day complaints (after 17:00) include stuffiness and warmth despite the cooling system running. CO2 monitoring shows the space at 1100 ppm by 17:00. Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with attention to demand-controlled ventilation. Primary cause: gradual buildup of heat through the day combined with insufficient end-of-day ventilation purge. The chilled beam system handles sensible heat but if the ventilation system is not demand-controlled (or is set to a fixed schedule), the fresh-air supply may not match the actual occupant heat output. CO2 at 1100 ppm indicates moderate accumulation — fresh-air rate around 8 L/s per person, which is design-minimum but insufficient at peak occupancy. Secondary causes: thermal mass charging — by end of day, all internal surfaces have absorbed heat and continue to release into the space; chilled beams may not adequately address latent load if humidity has risen; people accumulate over the day rather than have steady-state occupancy. Recommended: (1) measure fresh-air rate per person at peak occupancy; (2) consider demand-controlled ventilation linked to CO2 sensors; (3) increase free-cooling ventilation in evenings to flush stored heat; (4) review chilled beam capacity utilisation logs to confirm system is at design capacity; (5) implement an overnight ventilation purge if not present.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE TM21 (Indoor Air Quality)

question.text: A primary school classroom in Glasgow, top floor of a 1950s school. Pupils complain of being too cold in winter despite the radiator under the window being warm to the touch. The classroom is double-glazed (replaced 2010) and has a single occupied wall (north-facing). The class teacher reports the radiator is on a fixed 24-hour schedule (the BMS times have not been updated since pre-COVID). Diagnose.

answer.text: Apply TM52 with attention to control regime and building envelope. Primary cause: outdated 24-hour heating schedule means the radiator is undersized for the morning warm-up demand — the system has insufficient capacity to bring the classroom up to comfort temperature within the occupied period after overnight setback. By the time the room is warm enough for comfort, it is mid-morning. Secondary causes: top-floor exposure to roof heat loss; north-facing single-aspect orientation; double-glazing is good but not exceptional; radiator under the window provides convective warm-air rise but minimal radiant supplement at low level. Recommended: (1) update BMS to operate with an optimum-start strategy that begins heating earlier on cold mornings to ensure comfort at occupancy start; (2) check radiator output against winter heat-loss calculation for the classroom; (3) consider supplementing with a high-level radiant panel for morning warm-up; (4) measure floor and operative temperatures during the morning warm-up period; (5) ensure roof insulation is adequate.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide H (Building Control Systems); DfE BB101

question.text: A Manchester city-centre office on the 3rd floor of a 1990s refurbishment, north-facing perimeter zone with floor-to-ceiling glazing and finned-tube perimeter LPHW heating below the sill. In January and February, occupants within 1.5 m of the glazing report cold feet and draughts even though the room air temperature measured at desk height is 21.5°C. The BMS shows the perimeter heating valves fully open and flow temperature at 75°C. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and Guide A methodology and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: apply CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 operative temperature and local thermal discomfort criteria (PPD/PD from cold radiant asymmetry and draught), with TM52 as the overarching adaptive comfort framework even though the complaint is winter-dominant. Primary cause: cold radiant asymmetry and downdraught from the large single- or double-glazed facade — internal glazing surface temperature is likely 10–14°C against 21.5°C air, producing radiant asymmetry above the 10 K Guide A limit and a cold downdraught that the perimeter finned-tube emitter cannot fully counter because its upward convective plume is being entrained and pulled back to floor by the falling cold air sheet. Secondary causes: emitter undersized for the glazing U-value and height (typical 1990s finned-tube outputs of 400–600 W/m run are marginal against modern fully glazed perimeters); possible imbalance in the two-pipe circuit causing reduced flow at the index end; carpet/desk pedestals obstructing the convective plume. Recommended: (1) measure internal glass surface temperature, air temperature at ankle (0.1 m) and head (1.1 m) height, and air velocity at the glazing line — expect >0.2 m/s draught and >3 K vertical gradient; (2) calculate operative temperature and radiant asymmetry per Guide A; (3) hydraulic balance check and flow temperature/return DT review; (4) remediation — upgrade perimeter emitter to a trench heater or higher-output convector that sits directly under the glazing line to intercept the downdraught; (5) longer term, secondary glazing or low-e film to raise the internal surface temperature and reduce asymmetry.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A (2015) Chapter 1; CIBSE TM52 (2013); ISO 7730:2005

question.text: A 4-storey Bristol office, open-plan, served by 600x600 4-way blow ceiling cassette fan-coil units on a 3.6 m grid at a 2.8 m ceiling height. Occupants report cold-shoulder draught complaints in winter heating mode and 'stuffy' warm conditions in shoulder seasons, despite zone setpoints being met. Each cassette serves approximately 30 m² and runs on local thermostat with auto fan. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and Guide B3 methodology and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: apply CIBSE TM52 adaptive criteria for the shoulder-season warm complaints and Guide B3/Guide A local discomfort criteria (draught rate and vertical air temperature difference) for the winter draught complaints. Primary cause: mismatch between cassette throw characteristics and ceiling height/grid — 4-way blow cassettes at 2.8 m ceiling have rated throw of 3.5–4.5 m in cooling but only 2.0–2.5 m in heating because warm supply air buoyancy short-circuits back to the unit. In heating, the warm air rolls back along the ceiling and drops as a cold sheet at the wall/desk perimeter producing cold-shoulder draught; in shoulder seasons low-load operation cycles the unit off, supply mixing is poor and the space stratifies giving the 'stuffy' sensation even at setpoint. Secondary causes: auto fan control reduces fan speed at part load, further reducing throw and Coanda effect; cassette location on the grid does not align with occupant workstation positions; return air short-circuit on units with central return. Recommended: (1) smoke test cassette throw patterns in heating and cooling; (2) measure air velocity at 1.1 m and vertical temperature gradient (ankle-to-head) — Guide A limit 3 K; (3) log operative temperature against TM52 Criteria 1–3 over a representative week; (4) remediation — switch to constant fan speed (medium) during occupancy to maintain throw; (5) consider 4-pipe changeover or destratification fans; (6) where heating-dominant, supplement with perimeter LPHW or radiant panels and use cassettes primarily for cooling, which matches their aerodynamic strength.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide B3 (2016) Air Distribution; CIBSE Guide A (2015)

question.text: A Leeds professional services office, 5 floors, fan-coil units serving open-plan in nominal 200 m² zones each with a single zone thermostat near the lift core. Persistent complaints come from staff in the deep-plan interior who report being too cold while perimeter staff near the south windows complain of being too warm — both groups within the same FCU zone. Summer 2025, peak July. Diagnose under TM52 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: apply CIBSE TM52 with all three criteria (hours of exceedance, daily weighted exceedance, upper limit), but the dominant issue here is a zoning/control problem rather than absolute overheating capacity. Primary cause: single-thermostat zoning of a thermally inhomogeneous area — the thermostat near the lift core sees the average/interior load and calls for more cooling than the interior needs while still failing to satisfy the south-perimeter solar gain. The zone has effectively two distinct thermal demand regions (perimeter solar-dominated, interior internal-gain-dominated) being controlled by one sensor, so neither is satisfied. Secondary causes: FCU supply diffusers likely positioned without regard to the gain map so cool air is not preferentially delivered to perimeter; thermostat location near lift core also exposes it to transient gains from lift lobby occupants and warm shaft surfaces; no blinds management policy. Recommended: (1) heat-gain mapping of the zone separating solar, occupant, equipment and lighting components per Guide A; (2) spot measure operative temperature and run TM52 dynamic simulation by sub-zone (perimeter vs interior); (3) log thermostat sensor temperature against ground-truth sensors over a week; (4) remediation — split the FCU zone into perimeter and interior control zones with separate thermostats, ideally with VAV dampers or dedicated perimeter FCU; (5) reposition or add averaging sensors; (6) deploy internal blinds with automated control on the south facade to reduce perimeter peak gain by 40–60%.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2015); CIBSE Guide B2 (2016)

question.text: An Edinburgh financial services HQ uses displacement ventilation with low-level swirl diffusers along the perimeter, supplying air at 19°C with a target room temperature of 23°C. Occupants on a trading floor with high screen density (4 monitors per desk, ~250 W/desk) report cold ankles and warm heads, with several reporting headaches by mid-afternoon. Diagnose under TM52 and ISO 7730 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: apply CIBSE TM52 for overall adaptive comfort and ISO 7730 / CIBSE Guide A for local thermal discomfort — specifically vertical air temperature difference (head-to-ankle) and draught rate, both of which are characteristic failure modes of displacement ventilation when misapplied. Primary cause: heat gain density exceeds the displacement ventilation design envelope. Displacement systems are reliable up to ~25–40 W/m² sensible gain; trading floors at 250 W/desk on a 5–6 m² grid deliver 40–50 W/m² plus solar and lighting, pushing total gain well above the displacement comfort limit. The result is an excessive vertical temperature gradient (>3 K head-to-ankle, ISO 7730 Category B limit) and a thickening warm upper layer that traps contaminants and CO2 around head height, producing the 'warm head/cold ankle/headache' symptom triad. Secondary causes: supply temperature of 19°C is at the cool end (Guide B recommends >18°C for displacement to avoid ankle draught); diffuser face velocity likely too high producing local draught within 1 m near-zone; lack of any complementary high-level extract or chilled ceiling to remove the upper warm layer. Recommended: (1) measure vertical temperature gradient at 0.1, 0.6 and 1.1 m and draught rate within 1.5 m of diffusers per ISO 7730; (2) measure CO2 at breathing zone; (3) calculate displacement load per m² and compare with Guide B3 limits; (4) run TM52 dynamic simulation to confirm; (5) remediation — supplement displacement with chilled ceiling or passive chilled beams to remove the high sensible load while preserving displacement's IAQ benefit (a hybrid approach); (6) raise supply temperature to 20°C and increase near-zone diffuser area to reduce face velocity; (7) reduce desk equipment load where feasible.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); ISO 7730:2005; CIBSE Guide B3 (2016); CIBSE Guide A (2015)

question.text: A Cambridge research institute office in a 2018 BREEAM Excellent building uses mixed-mode ventilation: openable windows with motorised actuators in cool conditions, switching to mechanical cooling (AHU with chilled water coil) when external temperature exceeds 22°C or internal CO2 exceeds 1000 ppm. Occupants report repeated comfort complaints during the morning ramp-up on warm days (around 09:00–11:00) and in the late afternoon shoulder period, with reports of clammy air and oscillating temperatures. Diagnose under TM52 and TM52/TM59 mixed-mode guidance and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: apply CIBSE TM52 with the adaptive comfort model applicable during natural ventilation periods, and the static PMV/PPD model (Guide A / ISO 7730) during mechanical cooling — the mixed-mode transition itself must be assessed against both. Primary cause: poorly tuned changeover control creating hunting between modes during transition windows. At 09:00–11:00 the building is warming through the 22°C threshold while windows are still open; the AHU starts and stops as the threshold is crossed, producing oscillating temperature, fluctuating humidity (clammy sensation as cool, humid outside air interacts with cooling coil dehumidification) and occupant expectation mismatch — occupants in 'natural' mode tolerate wider bands but the intermittent cooling resets their expectation. Secondary causes: changeover hysteresis band too narrow (likely <1 K); no lockout between window actuators and AHU so both can operate simultaneously, wasting cooling and overcooling; CO2 setpoint of 1000 ppm triggers mechanical mode for IAQ reasons even when thermal conditions would be acceptable naturally; AHU supply air not dehumidified consistently at part-load. Recommended: (1) trend log internal/external temperature, RH, CO2, window position and AHU status over a 2-week warm period; (2) compute operative temperature and check against TM52 Criterion 1 separately for NV, mixed and MV hours; (3) measure local air velocity and RH during clammy periods; (4) remediation — widen changeover hysteresis to 2–3 K with minimum dwell time (e.g. 30 min) in each mode; (5) interlock window actuators to close before AHU cooling engages; (6) raise CO2 setpoint to 1200 ppm or decouple IAQ from thermal mode (use boost extract instead); (7) provide occupant signage/dashboard indicating current mode to manage expectation.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE AM10 (Natural Ventilation in Non-domestic Buildings); CIBSE Guide A (2015); ISO 7730:2005

question.text: A new-build two-bedroom flat in Manchester, fourth floor of a six-storey block, dual aspect east/west with MVHR. Occupants report the master bedroom reaches 27–29°C between 23:00 and 03:00 during a typical summer week, with no relief from opening windows because the street-facing west window has a 100mm restrictor and the east window backs onto a noisy communal walkway that the occupant keeps shut. Construction is high-performance: 0.18 W/m²K walls, triple glazing g-value 0.5, airtightness 3 m³/h·m². Diagnose under CIBSE TM59 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM59 (Design Methodology for the Assessment of Overheating Risk in Homes, 2017), which uses TM52 adaptive criteria but with predefined domestic occupancy profiles and the bedroom-specific rule that operative temperature must not exceed 26°C for more than 1% of annual occupied hours between 22:00 and 07:00. The reported 27–29°C overnight clearly breaches this. Primary cause: inability to achieve effective night purge ventilation. The west window restrictor limits effective opening area to roughly 5–8% of glazed area, and the east window is functionally closed due to noise/security — TM59 assumes openable areas can be relied upon, and where they cannot, the modelling must reflect actual use. Secondary causes: high envelope airtightness (3 m³/h·m²) and triple glazing trap accumulated daytime fabric gains; MVHR does not provide useful cooling and even with a summer bypass cannot match window purge rates; west-facing solar gain on triple glazing with g=0.5 is significant in late afternoon and re-radiates into the bedroom overnight via warm internal surfaces (elevated MRT). Recommended: (1) carry out a TM59 compliance assessment using realistic (not idealised) window opening assumptions reflecting noise and restrictor constraints; (2) measure operative temperature and MRT in the bedroom over a hot week alongside CO₂ to evidence MVHR cannot compensate; (3) install secure night-vent ventilators or acoustic trickle vents on the east elevation to allow safe purge against the walkway; (4) retrofit external solar shading or a high-performance solar control film to the west glazing to cut peak gain; (5) review window restrictor design with the freeholder — restrictors that release for ventilation while maintaining fall protection are widely available.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2015) Chapter 1

question.text: A Victorian mid-terrace house in Bristol has had a deep retrofit: 100mm internal wall insulation, loft insulation upgraded to 300mm, suspended timber floor insulated, double glazing throughout, and airtightness improved from circa 12 to 5 m³/h·m². The occupants report that since the retrofit the living room and rear kitchen-diner (south-facing patio doors) reach 28–30°C on warm days and stay above 25°C until midnight, whereas before the retrofit the house was comfortable. No mechanical ventilation was installed; the occupants rely on opening windows but the terrace has poor cross-ventilation because the front door opens onto a busy road. Diagnose under TM59 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM59 (2017) for domestic overheating risk, with reference to TM52 adaptive criteria — living spaces must not exceed Category II adaptive upper limit for more than 3% of occupied hours May–September. The retrofit has materially changed the thermal behaviour and a post-retrofit TM59 assessment should be carried out. Primary cause: drastically reduced infiltration (12 → 5 m³/h·m²) combined with no replacement purge ventilation strategy — the house previously 'self-purged' through leakage and chimneys, and that pathway has been closed without substitute. Secondary causes: south-facing patio doors deliver high solar gain into the rear room; internal wall insulation has reduced the exposed thermal mass that previously buffered daytime peaks (the masonry is now on the cold side of the insulation); inability to cross-ventilate because the front opening cannot be used safely or for noise reasons, leaving only single-sided ventilation at the rear. Recommended: (1) carry out a TM59 assessment of the post-retrofit dwelling using realistic window-opening profiles reflecting the road noise constraint; (2) monitor operative temperature in living room and bedrooms over a warm week and log window-open behaviour; (3) install external shading (awning, brise-soleil, or external blind) to the south patio doors — the highest-impact single measure; (4) provide a controllable purge route at the front of the house — acoustic background ventilators or a secure night-vent window unit — to re-enable cross-ventilation; (5) consider MVHR with summer bypass if a wider IAQ upgrade is justified, noting it does not replace the need for purge; (6) advise occupants on pre-cooling routines (open early morning, close and shade midday).
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE TM60 Good Practice in the Design of Homes (2018)

question.text: A top-floor mansard conversion above a converted Edwardian house in Islington, London. Two bedrooms with sloping ceilings, lined directly with 120mm PIR between rafters and a thin plasterboard finish; Velux-style rooflights face south-west and north-east with internal blackout blinds only. The flat has electric panel heaters and intermittent extract fans — no MVHR. Tenant reports bedrooms reach 30–32°C on hot days and remain above 27°C all night. Diagnose under TM59 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM59 (2017), noting that top-floor and mansard dwellings are flagged in TM59 and the GLA London Plan as elevated overheating risk and frequently fail the 1% bedroom criterion (Top ≤26°C, 22:00–07:00). A TM59 dynamic simulation with the actual rooflight schedule should be carried out. Primary cause: direct solar gain through unshaded south-west rooflights — rooflights typically have g-values around 0.5–0.6 and receive near-normal solar incidence in summer, delivering very high W/m² of glazing; internal blackout blinds absorb solar and re-radiate into the room, providing negligible solar mitigation. Secondary causes: low thermal mass — lightweight rafter-and-plasterboard build-up gives the room no buffering capacity; PIR at 120mm is below current best-practice for roof retrofit and the roof surface (often dark slate or tile) reaches very high temperatures in sun, driving conductive gain through any thermal bridges and ceiling junctions; limited stack/cross ventilation because rooflights open only a few degrees and there is no purpose-provided purge path. Recommended: (1) commission a TM59 assessment with realistic shading and opening assumptions; (2) measure internal operative temperature and external roof surface temperature over a hot week; (3) replace internal blackout blinds with external rooflight shading (external roller blinds or shutters designed for rooflights) — by far the highest-impact intervention; (4) specify solar-control glazing (g ≤ 0.35) when rooflights are next replaced; (5) provide a secure night-purge route — openable rooflights with insect screens and rain sensors, ideally automated for night cooling; (6) consider increasing roof insulation and adding a ventilated/reflective layer above the rafters at next re-roof to reduce conductive gain; (7) as a last resort, a small split AC unit serving the worst bedroom.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); GLA London Plan Guidance on Overheating (2023); CIBSE TM52 (2013)

question.text: A new-build single-aspect north-facing one-bed flat in Leeds, second floor of a five-storey block, completed 2023. Despite the north orientation, the tenant reports the living/kitchen room reaches 28°C from late afternoon onwards and the bedroom does not drop below 25°C overnight. The flat has an MVHR unit with summer bypass, a heat-interface unit (HIU) connected to a communal heating network, and exposed riser pipework running through a service cupboard adjacent to the kitchen. Diagnose under TM59 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM59 (2017) with reference to CIBSE CP1 (Heat Networks Code of Practice, 2020), which addresses overheating from communal heat network distribution losses — a well-documented cause of overheating in north-facing or otherwise low-solar-gain flats on heat networks. Primary cause: heat gains from the communal heating distribution — uninsulated or under-insulated HIU and primary risers in the service cupboard radiate heat continuously into the flat year-round; CP1 reports typical distribution losses of 50–150 W per metre of poorly insulated primary, and HIUs themselves can dissipate 50–100 W when idle. North-facing single-aspect with no solar load makes these internal gains dominant. Secondary causes: single-aspect layout prevents any cross-ventilation, so MVHR (which provides no useful cooling) is the only ventilation pathway and bypass alone cannot remove accumulated internal gains; kitchen appliance and occupancy gains add to the load; the flat's high airtightness and insulation retain heat overnight. Recommended: (1) carry out a TM59 assessment including realistic HIU and riser gain inputs per CP1 guidance — many original TM59 models omit these and pass; (2) measure surface temperatures of the HIU, risers, and service cupboard wall, and log air temperature in adjacent rooms over a week; (3) upgrade insulation on primary pipework and HIU casing to CP1 standards; review whether the network flow temperature can be reduced in summer (DHW-only mode); (4) ventilate the service cupboard directly to outside if feasible; (5) review MVHR commissioning — confirm summer bypass operates correctly and consider boost purge ventilation overnight; (6) consider openable secure night vents to enable purge given the single-aspect constraint.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); CIBSE CP1 Heat Networks Code of Practice (2020); CIBSE TM52 (2013)

question.text: A 1970s end-of-terrace house in Reading retrofitted with external wall insulation (150mm EPS), an air source heat pump, and a new MVHR system. The south-west gable wall is the largest external elevation. Occupants report the upstairs landing and front bedroom (south-west facing, two openable windows) reach 29°C on warm days and the MVHR 'doesn't seem to help'. Windows are kept open day and night but there is no obvious cross-ventilation route upstairs because the rear bedroom window is small and high-level. Diagnose under TM59 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM59 (2017) using TM52 adaptive criteria; the property is a retrofit dwelling and TM59 is the relevant framework for assessing residual overheating risk post-retrofit. Primary cause: solar gain on the south-west gable and front bedroom windows is the dominant load, peaking 14:00–19:00 when external air is also at its hottest, so daytime window opening admits warm air rather than cooling. The occupant's belief that 'the MVHR doesn't help' is correct — MVHR is a ventilation system, not a cooling system, and its summer bypass only avoids heat recovery; it does not remove solar or fabric gains. Secondary causes: poor upstairs cross-ventilation geometry — small high-level rear window cannot drive useful single-sided or cross flow against the larger SW openings; EWS retrofit has reduced infiltration and shifted thermal mass to the inside of the masonry, which helps buffer peaks but also retains heat overnight if purge is inadequate; landing acts as a heat sink from the staircase stack effect carrying ground-floor gains upward. Recommended: (1) perform a TM59 assessment of the retrofitted dwelling with realistic opening areas and shading; (2) monitor operative temperature, window-open state, and external air temperature over a hot spell to show when opening windows is counter-productive; (3) install external shading on south-west windows — external roller blinds or shutters are the highest-impact measure; (4) educate occupants on a 'closed during the day, open at night' purge strategy now that the dwelling has useful thermal mass; (5) consider enlarging or adding a secure openable rear upstairs vent to enable effective cross/stack ventilation overnight; (6) confirm MVHR summer bypass is functioning and increase summer purge airflow if available; (7) plant or pergola shading to the SW gable as a longer-term measure.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM59 (2017); CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2015)

question.text: A primary school classroom in Reading, Year 4 cohort of 30 pupils plus teacher and TA, south-facing with internal blinds and high-level openable windows controlled by teacher. Building was refurbished in 2019 to BB101 standards with cross-ventilation via corridor transom vents. Teacher reports the room reaches 27–28°C from late May through July, pupils visibly drowsy after lunch, CO2 logger shows 1800–2200 ppm in afternoon sessions. The mechanical extract serving the corridor was found running but the transom vents were closed by the cleaning contractor. Diagnose under BB101 and CIBSE TM52 and recommend investigation and remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply BB101 (2018) which uses the CIBSE TM52 adaptive overheating criteria for naturally ventilated school spaces, assessed against the three TM52 criteria (Hours of Exceedance >3%, Daily Weighted Exceedance, Upper Limit Temperature) during occupied hours, alongside BB101 indoor air quality limits for naturally ventilated classrooms (daily average CO2 below 1500 ppm, with excursions above 2000 ppm permitted for no more than 20 consecutive minutes a day; the tighter 1000 ppm daily average applies to mechanically ventilated spaces). Primary cause: failure of the designed cross-ventilation path — the closed corridor transoms have collapsed the single-sided to cross-flow conversion, reducing effective ventilation rate to perhaps 2–3 l/s/person against the BB101 minimum of 5 l/s/person, explaining both the CO2 excursion and heat build-up. Secondary causes: south-facing solar gain through glazing with internal-only blinds (which re-radiate absorbed heat into the room rather than rejecting it externally); high internal gains from 32 occupants (~2.5 kW sensible) plus IT and lighting; post-lunch metabolic peak coinciding with peak solar. Recommended: (1) commission a week-long monitoring campaign logging dry-bulb, globe, CO2 and window/transom position, then run TM52 assessment in dynamic simulation; (2) urgent operational fix — issue facilities instruction to keep corridor transoms open during occupied hours and lock them open mechanically; (3) re-commission the night purge sequence (open high-level vents overnight when external <internal and >12°C); (4) replace internal blinds with external brise-soleil or mid-pane blinds on south elevation; (5) provide teacher with a simple CO2 traffic-light display to manage window opening behaviour.
answer.citation: BB101: Ventilation, thermal comfort and indoor air quality in schools (ESFA, 2018); CIBSE TM52 (2013)

question.text: A 350-seat university lecture theatre in Manchester, raked seating, no external windows, served by a dedicated AHU with mixing box and DX cooling coil. During back-to-back 50-minute lectures from 10:00–16:00, students at the rear upper rows complain of stuffiness and heat by minute 30, while the front rows feel cool and draughty. BMS logs show supply air at 16°C constant, return air rising from 22°C to 26°C across the session, and CO2 climbing from 600 to 1600 ppm. The AHU is at design airflow. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 / Guide A and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM52 for overheating assessment combined with CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 for operative temperature and air distribution effectiveness, and Guide B2 for ventilation effectiveness in deep-plan/raked spaces. The diagnosis is fundamentally one of stratification and air distribution failure rather than plant capacity. Primary cause: thermal stratification in the raked theatre — warm exhaled and body-plume air rises and accumulates at the upper rear rows where the high-level extract is either undersized or poorly located, while cool supply air from front/low-level diffusers short-circuits across the front rows. Effective ventilation rate at the rear is therefore far below the nominal per-seat design figure, evidenced by the CO2 rise to 1600 ppm against a likely design of <1000 ppm. Secondary causes: constant-volume 16°C supply oversized for the part-load early period creates front-row draught (PD likely >20%), while the load-following capability is absent — the AHU does not modulate to occupancy; metabolic gain from 350 students (~25 kW sensible) concentrated in the upper third of the room volume; possible re-circulation damper position reducing fresh air fraction. Recommended: (1) CO2 and temperature gradient survey — log at floor, mid and high level across rear and front during a full lecture day; (2) smoke/tracer test to visualise actual air paths and confirm stratification; (3) TM52 dynamic model with stratified zoning rather than fully-mixed assumption; (4) increase high-level extract at rear, ideally with displacement ventilation strategy supplying at low velocity at floor and extracting at ceiling; (5) introduce CO2-based demand-controlled ventilation and raise supply temperature to 18–19°C to eliminate front-row draught; (6) review minimum fresh air fraction against BB101/Approved Document F equivalent for higher education.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2021) Environmental Design, Chapter 1; CIBSE Guide B2 Ventilation and Ductwork

question.text: A 1960s university library in Bristol, four storeys, deep-plan, with a 2015 mixed-mode retrofit: openable windows on the perimeter and a central VAV system serving the deep zones. The top-floor reading room (south and west glazing, exposed concrete soffit retained for thermal mass) overheats in September every year, with operative temperatures reaching 29°C between 13:00 and 18:00. Students complain and migrate downstairs. The BMS shows the VAV in cooling mode at full open, perimeter windows have automated actuators that are closed because external temperature exceeds the 24°C changeover setpoint. Diagnose under TM52 and recommend.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply CIBSE TM52 against all three criteria, with particular focus on the mixed-mode changeover logic per CIBSE AM13 (Mixed Mode Ventilation Systems). The September timing is diagnostic — it points to a thermal mass / changeover interaction rather than a peak-summer plant capacity problem. Primary cause: mis-configured mixed-mode changeover. Closing windows at 24°C external lock the building into mechanical-only mode but the exposed concrete soffit has charged with heat over preceding warm days (heatwave tail typical of September) and is now re-radiating to the space — elevating mean radiant temperature 2–3 K above air temperature and pushing operative temperature beyond TM52 Cat II limits even when supply air is at setpoint. The VAV cooling is countering air temperature but not the radiant load from the warm slab. Secondary causes: top-floor location subject to roof heat gain and warmest stratified air in the building; south/west solar gain in September has low sun angle bypassing any horizontal shading; loss of night cooling because automated windows are closed when external <internal at night due to the daytime changeover lock; absence of a night-purge sub-strategy. Recommended: (1) measure surface temperature of soffit and globe temperature alongside air temperature for a fortnight; (2) calculate operative temperature and run TM52 with realistic mixed-mode control schedules; (3) re-programme changeover to permit night-purge window opening whenever Tint > Text + 2K and Text > 12°C, irrespective of daytime mode; (4) raise daytime changeover threshold and/or use enthalpy-based switching; (5) add external solar shading or solar-control film to south/west glazing for low-angle September sun; (6) verify BMS dead-bands so VAV and windows do not fight each other.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE AM13 Mixed Mode Ventilation Systems (2000); CIBSE Guide A (2021)

question.text: A new-build primary school in Norwich, single-storey, completed 2022 to BB101 with hybrid ventilation (wind cowls with low-level supply louvres and assisted extract fans). A north-facing Year 2 classroom of 28 pupils reports the opposite of overheating — children are cold in October and February, sitting in coats, with reported air temperatures of 17–18°C during morning lessons despite the LPHW underfloor heating system running. The TRV-equivalent room sensor reads 21°C at high level. Cold draughts are reported around feet. Diagnose under BB101 and CIBSE Guide A and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Methodology: Apply BB101 (2018) winter comfort criteria (operative temperature 19–21°C for teaching spaces) and CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 for local thermal discomfort assessment, specifically draught risk (DR), vertical air temperature difference (head-to-ankle <3K per ISO 7730 Cat B) and radiant asymmetry. Primary cause: cold-air dumping from the wind cowl / low-level supply louvres in winter — un-tempered outside air at 5–10°C is being driven by wind pressure through the supply path directly to the occupied zone, creating high air velocity at ankle level and a strong vertical stratification (sensor at high level reads 21°C while ankle level is 17°C). Underfloor heating is delivering its setpoint but the room sensor is mis-located and the heat is being short-circuited by the cold incoming air sliding across the floor. Secondary causes: room sensor location at high level gives false satisfaction signal to the heating controls, throttling output; possible failure or absence of supply air pre-heat / tempering coil that BB101 hybrid designs typically require for winter operation; underfloor heating slow response cannot counter sudden cold influx during gusty conditions; control logic likely treats ventilation as demand-driven on CO2 only without minimum-temperature override. Recommended: (1) measure vertical temperature gradient (ankle, seated head, standing head) and air velocity at ankle level over a cold week, calculate Draught Rate per ISO 7730; (2) verify supply air temperature entering the room and check for any pre-heat coil operation; (3) relocate room sensor to seated occupied-zone height (1.1 m) or use a globe sensor; (4) commission a winter low-flow ventilation setpoint with CO2-modulated control, ensuring supply tempering to minimum 16°C before discharge; (5) review wind cowl damper modulation — many hybrid systems require winter throttling; (6) confirm BB101 minimum 3 l/s/person is met without overshoot.
answer.citation: BB101 (2018); CIBSE Guide A (2021) Chapter 1; BS EN ISO 7730 (2005)

question.text: A 28-bed acute medical ward in a Leeds NHS hospital, single-corridor layout with south-facing patient bays, built 2008. During the July 2022 heatwave, nursing staff report patient bay temperatures reached 29–30°C in the afternoon. The ward has mechanical ventilation supplying 6 ach tempered to 21°C but no active cooling on the ward floor (cooling reserved for theatres and critical care per HTM 03-01 specialist area requirements). Patients are elderly, frail, and largely immobile. Openable windows are restrictor-limited to 100mm. Diagnose under TM52 and recommend remediation appropriate to a healthcare setting.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 with reference to HTM 03-01 Part A, which establishes that general ward areas in the UK are typically ventilation-only (not cooled) but recognises summertime overheating risk and recommends the 28°C / 1% occupied-hours threshold for non-clinical areas, with stricter limits for vulnerable patients. TM52's three criteria are applied with the recognition that bed-bound elderly patients cannot adapt (cannot remove clothing layers freely, cannot relocate, have impaired thermoregulation), so the adaptive comfort model is only partially applicable — operative temperature is the key metric. Primary cause: south-facing solar gain through patient bay glazing combined with absence of active cooling and ventilation supply temperature (21°C) insufficient to offset peak gains during heatwave conditions when external dry-bulb exceeds 30°C. Secondary causes: window restrictors (fall prevention per HTM compliance) limit purge ventilation effectiveness; high internal gains from medical equipment and bed-bound patient metabolic load; mechanical ventilation cooling coil (if present) sized only for tempering, not summer peak. Recommended: (1) measure operative temperature and globe temperature in worst-affected bays across a hot week and assess against TM52 criteria and HTM 03-01 thresholds; (2) dynamic thermal modelling with heatwave weather file (DSY1/DSY2) per TM49; (3) retrofit external solar shading or solar-control film on south elevation as primary structural fix; (4) install local cooling (split-system or chilled water fan-coils) for vulnerable patient bays — HTM 03-01 permits this where clinical risk assessment supports it; (5) interim measures during heatwaves: portable HEPA-filtered cooling units, increased hydration protocols, redistribution of vulnerable patients to cooler north-facing bays.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); HTM 03-01 Part A (Specialised Ventilation for Healthcare Premises, 2021); CIBSE TM49 (Design Summer Years)

question.text: A 40-resident care home for the elderly in Bournemouth, two-storey 1990s build with gas-fired radiator heating and trickle-vent natural ventilation. Residents complain of being cold in the communal lounge during winter mornings (reporting they 'cannot feel their feet') despite the room air temperature meeting the 23°C setpoint measured at the thermostat on the internal wall. Mean resident age 84, largely sedentary, dressed in cardigans and indoor footwear. Diagnose under CIBSE Guide A and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 (Environmental criteria for design), which recognises that elderly sedentary occupants require operative temperatures of 23–25°C (compared with 21–23°C for general adult populations) due to reduced metabolic rate (~1.0 met or below), thinner subcutaneous fat, impaired peripheral circulation, and reduced thermoregulatory response. ISO 7730 PMV/PPD analysis should be applied with elderly-appropriate metabolic and clothing assumptions. Primary cause: cold radiant asymmetry and low surface temperatures — the thermostat reads air temperature on a warm internal wall but the operative temperature near external walls, single-glazed/older double-glazed windows, and uninsulated ground floor is materially lower. Cold floor surface temperature (likely 17–18°C) drives local discomfort at the feet, which Guide A identifies as a specific local discomfort parameter (floor temperature should be 19–29°C, ideally 21–23°C for sedentary occupants). Secondary causes: radiator emitters sized for 21°C target rather than 24°C; trickle vents introducing cold draughts at ankle level; potential radiator stratification leaving floor zone undercooled; thermostat location not representative of occupied zone. Recommended: (1) measure operative temperature, floor surface temperature, and radiant asymmetry at seated head/ankle heights in occupied positions per ISO 7726; (2) calculate PMV/PPD with met=1.0 and clo=1.0 inputs; (3) reposition thermostat or add a remote sensor in the occupied zone and raise setpoint to 24°C; (4) install floor insulation or carpet/underlay upgrade to raise floor surface temperature; (5) consider low-temperature underfloor heating retrofit or higher-output radiators; (6) review trickle vent positioning and consider MVHR to eliminate cold draughts while maintaining IAQ.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A (Environmental Design, 2015) Chapter 1; ISO 7730:2005; ISO 7726

question.text: A GP surgery waiting room in Manchester, ground floor of a converted Victorian terrace, single large room (60m²) with a north-facing bay window and one external wall. Patients report being uncomfortably warm and stuffy by mid-morning even in October, while the receptionist behind the glazed screen on the internal wall reports being cold. The system is a single gas combi boiler feeding two radiators with a wall thermostat in the reception area set to 21°C. Occupancy varies 5–25 people. Diagnose under TM52/Guide A and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 for design criteria with TM52 adaptive principles for transient overheating assessment, recognising that a GP waiting room has highly variable occupancy and a mixed vulnerable population (elderly, infants, unwell adults) with diverse clothing and metabolic states. The simultaneous hot-and-cold complaints are a classic zoning failure. Primary cause: single-zone control with thermostat in the unoccupied/low-gain reception area cannot satisfy a waiting room with variable internal gains (25 people at ~100 W sensible each = 2.5 kW peak) plus no mechanical ventilation to remove CO₂ and moisture. The thermostat sees the cool reception (behind glazed screen, low occupancy) and continues calling for heat while the waiting area overheats from occupant gains. Secondary causes: absence of mechanical ventilation produces CO₂ build-up (likely >1500 ppm) driving 'stuffiness' perception independent of dry-bulb temperature; radiators sized for fabric losses only, not modulating to occupant gains; glazed reception screen creates a thermally isolated micro-zone; potential infection-control concern (post-COVID guidance favours higher ventilation rates in primary care waiting areas). Recommended: (1) measure CO₂, operative temperature, and relative humidity across a full clinic session in both zones; (2) calculate PMV/PPD for both areas with representative occupant profiles; (3) split the heating zone with a TRV-controlled approach and relocate or add a second thermostat in the waiting area; (4) install mechanical ventilation (MVHR or demand-controlled extract with trickle supply) sized for 10 L/s/person per Building Regulations Part F and HTM 03-01 primary care guidance; (5) consider a small reversible heat pump or fan-coil for waiting area cooling/heating with CO₂-linked boost; (6) review thermostat setpoint downward to 20°C once ventilation is improved.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2015) Chapter 1; Building Regulations Approved Document F (2021); HTM 03-01 Part A (2021)

question.text: A 12-bed elderly mental health ward in a Birmingham mental health trust, recently refurbished 2023 with sealed windows (anti-ligature, no opening) and a new VAV system supplying 10 ach with cooling. Despite the BMS showing room air temperature held at 22°C year-round, several patients with dementia are reported by staff as agitated, removing clothing, and complaining of being 'too hot' in the afternoons, while others (in the same bay) huddle under blankets complaining of cold draughts. HTM 03-01 compliance was certified at handover. Diagnose under TM52, Guide A, and ISO 7730 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide A Chapter 1 local discomfort criteria, ISO 7730 PMV/PPD with draught rating (DR) calculation, and TM52 for any solar-driven overheating periods, with HTM 03-01 Part A confirming the ventilation rate is correct for the clinical specialism. The fact that BMS air temperature is at setpoint while contradictory comfort complaints arise within the same space points strongly to local discomfort parameters (draught, vertical air temperature gradient, radiant asymmetry) rather than bulk air temperature. Primary cause: high air change rate (10 ach) combined with cooling supply air temperature delivers elevated air velocity at occupant level — ISO 7730 draught rating likely exceeds 20% (Category B failure) in seats directly under diffusers, perceived as 'cold draughts'. Secondary causes: (a) dementia patients have impaired ability to communicate accurate thermal sensation and may misattribute discomfort sources, removing clothing in response to draught-induced skin cooling cycles; (b) solar gain through sealed glazing in afternoon raises mean radiant temperature in window-adjacent positions while diffuser-adjacent positions experience cool jet, producing simultaneous hot/cold complaints across the same bay; (c) sealed windows eliminate any adaptive opportunity (no personal control), violating adaptive comfort principles even though TM52 strict criteria may be met; (d) anti-ligature constraints limit traditional remediation (no portable fans, no easily-adjustable diffusers). Recommended: (1) measure air velocity at 0.1m, 0.6m, 1.1m heights, operative temperature, and mean radiant temperature at multiple bed positions per ISO 7726; (2) calculate ISO 7730 PMV, PPD, draught rating (DR), and vertical air temperature difference for each position; (3) re-balance VAV minimum airflow rates to lowest level consistent with HTM 03-01 ach requirement; (4) replace high-velocity diffusers with low-velocity displacement or swirl diffusers designed for healthcare; (5) raise cooling supply air temperature and add reheat where needed to reduce velocity at occupant zone; (6) add internal solar shading (anti-ligature compliant) on affected elevations; (7) engage clinical staff in interpreting patient behavioural signals as environmental indicators since verbal feedback is unreliable in this population.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (2015) Chapter 1; ISO 7730:2005; ISO 7726:1998; HTM 03-01 Part A (2021)

question.text: A flagship retail unit on Oxford Street, London, occupies a double-height ground floor with a fully glazed shopfront (8m high, south-east facing) and a recessed entrance with automatic sliding doors that remain open during trading hours (09:00–21:00). Staff at till positions near the entrance report cold draughts in winter mornings and overheating from 11:00 onwards in summer; customers near the back of the store complain of stuffiness. The unit has a 4-pipe fan coil system with ceiling diffusers at 4.5m and an air curtain over the entrance that staff report as 'weak'. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and recommend investigation and remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 for the non-domestic retail space, with reference to CIBSE Guide A for entrance design and air curtain performance. Methodology: assess Criterion 1 (Hours of Exceedance), Criterion 2 (Daily Weighted Exceedance) and Criterion 3 (Upper Limit Temperature) zonally — front-of-store, mid-store and back-of-store should be modelled separately as they experience distinct microclimates. Primary cause: the combination of large south-east glazed shopfront delivering 300–500 W/m² of solar gain through morning to early afternoon, and an underperforming air curtain failing to seal the open entrance — allowing infiltration of warm humid external air in summer and cold air in winter. Air curtain discharge velocity is likely below the 8–10 m/s required to maintain a stable jet over an 8m-high opening, and the unit may be sized for a standard 2.4m doorway rather than a double-height void. Secondary causes: stratification in the double-height volume concentrates warm air at high level where ceiling diffusers recirculate it; fan coil throw at 4.5m mounting height is inadequate to reach occupied zone at till positions; mean radiant temperature near the glazing is elevated by direct solar and re-radiation from sunlit floor finishes. Recommended: (1) measure air velocity and temperature profiles at the entrance threshold across a day and across seasons; (2) measure operative temperature and MRT at till positions and back-of-store; (3) CFD or dynamic simulation of the double-height volume with realistic door-open infiltration rates; (4) upgrade or recommission the air curtain — likely a high-performance industrial unit sized for the actual opening height with twin discharge; (5) apply solar control film or internal motorised blinds to the upper portion of the shopfront where merchandising allows; (6) introduce low-level supply diffusers or destratification fans to address the occupied zone directly.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (Environmental Design, 2015), Section 1 and Section 4 on entrance design

question.text: A four-storey shopping centre atrium in Manchester, with retail units opening onto the atrium void on each floor and a glazed roof (40% of plan area). The centre management reports persistent complaints from upper-floor retailers (levels 3 and 4) of overheating during sunny days from May to September, with measured air temperatures of 28–30°C at level 4 versus 23–24°C at ground level. The atrium uses a displacement ventilation strategy with low-level supply at ground floor and high-level extract through motorised roof vents controlled to open above 25°C. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 for the non-domestic mixed-mode atrium, with reference to CIBSE AM10 (Natural Ventilation in Non-Domestic Buildings) for stack-driven design. Methodology: assess the three TM52 criteria at each level separately, as the atrium exhibits strong vertical stratification — a single 'atrium average' temperature will mask upper-level non-compliance. Primary cause: classic stack effect concentrating warm air at upper levels, combined with solar gain through the roof glazing creating a 'solar chimney' that drives buoyancy. The displacement strategy works as designed for the ground floor but the upper floors sit within the warm upper plume rather than the cool lower reservoir. Roof vent opening setpoint of 25°C is likely too high and the free vent area insufficient to discharge the combined buoyancy and solar load. Secondary causes: retail unit doors open onto the atrium expose retailers to the stratified atrium air; roof glazing g-value likely 0.4–0.6 admits substantial solar gain directly onto upper-level balconies; thermal mass of the atrium structure re-radiates absorbed solar in the afternoon; potential cross-contamination from restaurant kitchens venting into the atrium volume. Recommended: (1) install vertical temperature profile loggers (ground, L1, L2, L3, L4, roof apex) over a hot week to quantify stratification gradient; (2) measure roof vent free area and discharge coefficient and compare with CIBSE AM10 sizing for the actual solar and occupancy loads; (3) dynamic thermal model with CFD coupling to verify stack flow rates; (4) lower roof vent opening setpoint to 22–23°C and add modulating control; (5) increase free vent area or add powered assist extract at high level for peak conditions; (6) apply solar control to roof glazing (fritted film, external shading or switchable glazing) to reduce solar chimney effect; (7) consider supplementary local cooling at upper retail unit thresholds.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE AM10 (Natural Ventilation in Non-Domestic Buildings, 2005); CIBSE Guide A

question.text: A casual dining restaurant in a Birmingham shopping centre, located adjacent to the food court atrium with an open-fronted servery and a semi-open kitchen visible to diners. Front-of-house staff and diners at tables within 4m of the kitchen pass-through report overheating year-round, with measured air temperatures of 26–28°C even in winter while the rest of the restaurant sits at 22°C. The kitchen has a Class I canopy hood with make-up air supply at 80% of extract, and the dining area is served by a separate VRF system that runs at full cooling continuously. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 for the dining area combined with CIBSE Guide B2 and DW/172 (Specification for Kitchen Ventilation Systems) for the kitchen-dining interface. Methodology: TM52 Criteria 1–3 assessed in the affected zone within 4m of the pass-through, recognising that this zone behaves as a mixed kitchen-dining microclimate distinct from the main restaurant. Primary cause: kitchen heat and convective plume spillover into the dining area. With make-up air at only 80% of extract, the kitchen runs at negative pressure and draws replacement air from the dining area — but the canopy capture efficiency is likely insufficient for the cooking line, allowing convective heat (3–8 kW per cooking station) and radiant heat from hot surfaces to escape the canopy envelope and migrate into the dining zone. Secondary causes: radiant heat transfer from visible hot cooking surfaces directly elevates mean radiant temperature at nearby tables (MRT likely 3–6 K above air temperature); VRF system responds to air temperature sensor but cannot offset radiant load; potential additional gain from atrium spillover via the open-fronted servery; make-up air may be untreated outside air being drawn through the dining space. Recommended: (1) measure air velocity at the canopy face to verify capture velocity meets DW/172 (typically 0.25–0.5 m/s); (2) measure operative temperature and MRT at affected tables across a service period; (3) smoke or tracer gas test to visualise plume escape from canopy; (4) thermal imaging of kitchen-dining boundary to identify radiant sources; (5) increase canopy extract rate and rebalance make-up air to 85–90% of extract, with dedicated tempered make-up air delivered into the kitchen rather than drawn through dining; (6) extend canopy overhang or add side curtains to improve capture; (7) install a physical or air-curtain barrier at the pass-through; (8) consider radiant shielding (glass screen) between cooking line and nearest tables.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide B2 (Ventilation and Ductwork); BESA DW/172 (Specification for Kitchen Ventilation Systems, 2018)

question.text: A department store in Leeds occupies a refurbished Victorian building with a new triple-height glazed atrium inserted at the centre of the ground floor cosmetics hall. The atrium is south-facing with a sloped glazed roof. Beauty consultants working at counters directly beneath and adjacent to the atrium roof report severe overheating (complaints of 'sunburn through the glass') from late morning onwards in spring and summer, despite the comfort cooling system maintaining 22°C air temperature at the counters. The store uses overhead 4-pipe fan coils with displacement-style supply. Diagnose under CIBSE TM52 and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE TM52 for the non-domestic retail space, with reference to CIBSE Guide A Section 1 on radiant asymmetry and operative temperature, and ISO 7730 for local thermal discomfort criteria. Methodology: standard air-temperature compliance (the 22°C measurement) is misleading here — TM52 criteria should be assessed using operative temperature, and ISO 7730 radiant asymmetry limits (a warm ceiling is the binding case here at <5 K; <10 K applies to a cool vertical surface and <23 K to a warm wall) should be checked. Primary cause: direct beam solar radiation through the sloped south-facing atrium roof glazing landing on staff at counters — at solar noon in June this can deliver 600–800 W/m² of direct radiation onto exposed skin and counter surfaces, which is experienced as intense radiant discomfort regardless of air temperature. The 'sunburn' complaint is literal: untreated glass transmits significant UV. Secondary causes: solar absorbed by counter and floor finishes re-radiates as long-wave to elevate mean radiant temperature; sloped glazing has higher solar transmittance than vertical glazing for high-angle summer sun; air-temperature-controlled fan coil system cannot respond to radiant load; possible solar chimney effect in the atrium volume creating stratification that the fan coils then have to overcome. Recommended: (1) measure operative temperature, MRT and plane radiant asymmetry at affected counter positions; (2) measure solar irradiance at counter level across a day; (3) verify glazing specification (g-value, UV transmittance) against design intent; (4) primary remediation is solar control at the roof — external motorised blinds, fritted or ceramic-printed glazing, switchable (electrochromic) glazing, or a fixed brise-soleil designed for summer cut-off; (5) interim measure: internal motorised roller blinds at high level, or relocation of affected counters away from direct beam zone; (6) consider radiant cooling panels at high level to counter the elevated MRT; (7) review fan coil zoning so the affected counters have independent control responding to local conditions.
answer.citation: CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE Guide A (Environmental Design, 2015), Section 1; BS EN ISO 7730 (2005)
