question.text: A university chemistry teaching laboratory in Manchester, fitted with 12 constant-volume fume cupboards (0.5 m/s face velocity) and a single-pass supply air system providing 8 ACH. During winter term, occupants complain of cold draughts at workstations adjacent to the fume cupboards, with reported air temperatures of 18°C at standing height despite the AHU supply setpoint of 21°C. The lab is on the north elevation of a 1990s building with single-glazed Crittall windows. Diagnose under TM52 and CIBSE Guide A, and recommend investigation and remediation steps.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide A (Environmental Design) for laboratory comfort criteria alongside TM52 principles, noting that laboratories with fume cupboards have inherently high ventilation rates that dominate the thermal environment. Primary cause: the high extract rate driven by 12 constant-volume fume cupboards (typically 600–900 l/s per cupboard at 0.5 m/s face velocity through a 1m sash) creates a make-up air demand of roughly 8,000–10,000 l/s, which the single-pass supply system delivers as a large volume of tempered but cool air, generating perceptible draughts (>0.2 m/s local air velocity) at occupied workstations. Secondary causes: cold radiant asymmetry from single-glazed Crittall windows on north elevation lowers mean radiant temperature by 2–4 K below air temperature; supply diffuser selection likely sized for lower ACH and now operating outside their throw/induction envelope; no heat recovery on extract leads to cold supply on cold days. Recommended: (1) measure local air velocity, air temperature and globe temperature at seated and standing heights per ISO 7730 draught risk (DR index); (2) survey fume cupboard sash positions and face velocities — many may be running with sashes fully open unnecessarily; (3) convert constant-volume cupboards to variable-air-volume (VAV) with sash sensors to reduce extract when not in active use; (4) install run-around coil or thermal wheel heat recovery on extract (with appropriate cross-contamination safeguards); (5) upgrade glazing or add secondary glazing to reduce radiant asymmetry; (6) reselect supply diffusers for high-induction low-velocity performance at occupied zone.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A (Environmental Design, 2015), Section 1; CIBSE TM52 (2013); BS EN 14175 (Fume Cupboards); ISO 7730 (Draught Risk)

question.text: A community leisure centre swimming pool in Leeds, 25m main pool with water temperature held at 29°C, pool hall air temperature setpoint 30°C, 60% RH. Complaints from spectators on the poolside seating area of feeling clammy and stuffy, and the centre manager reports persistent condensation on the north-facing curtain walling and corrosion staining on steel roof fixings. The AHU is a dedicated pool unit with run-around coil heat recovery but no dehumidification beyond ventilation dilution. Diagnose under CIBSE Guide G and TM52 principles, and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide G (Public Health and Plumbing Engineering) and Section 2 of CIBSE Guide A for swimming pool environmental design, supported by TM52 for occupant comfort assessment. The key design parameter is dewpoint control, not simply RH: at 30°C and 60% RH, dewpoint is approximately 21.4°C, which is close to or above the inside surface temperature of north-facing single- or double-glazed curtain walling in a Leeds winter, causing surface condensation. Primary cause: insufficient dehumidification capacity — the ventilation dilution strategy cannot remove sufficient moisture during cold weather when occupancy and evaporation peak, allowing dewpoint to rise above the cold envelope surface temperatures. Secondary causes: spectator area is at the same air condition as the pool hall (30°C, high humidity) but spectators are dressed for outdoor conditions (clo ~1.0) leading to high PMV and clammy sensation — guidance recommends a separate, drier, cooler spectator zone; pool hall air temperature should be 1 K above water temperature (i.e. 30°C is correct) to suppress evaporation, but without dehumidification the moisture load is unmanageable. Recommended: (1) measure dewpoint and surface temperatures at the curtain walling using psychrometer and IR thermography over a cold week; (2) calculate the moisture balance (evaporation rate ≈ 200 g/m²·h for an unoccupied pool, higher when active); (3) install active dehumidification — either a heat-pump dehumidifier integrated with the AHU or a separate desiccant unit — to maintain dewpoint below 15°C; (4) provide a separately conditioned spectator gallery at ~24°C, 50% RH; (5) upgrade north curtain walling thermal performance and check for thermal bridges at fixings; (6) verify pool cover use during unoccupied hours to reduce baseline evaporation.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide G (Public Health and Plumbing Engineering); CIBSE Guide A (2015), Section 2 (Swimming pools); CIBSE TM52 (2013); Swimming Pool Water Treatment Advisory Group (PWTAG) guidance

question.text: A financial services tenant in Canary Wharf has converted a 40 m² meeting room on the office floor into a server room hosting two cabinets (~12 kW total IT load) using a wall-mounted split DX unit set to 18°C. Adjacent open-plan office occupants complain of cold draughts and noise along the partition wall, while IT staff complain that the server room itself fluctuates between 15°C and 28°C with intermittent high-temperature alarms. The office cooling is a 4-pipe FCU system on a CAV outdoor air supply. Diagnose under TM52 / CIBSE Guide A and recommend remediation.

answer.text: Apply CIBSE Guide A (Section 1, comfort criteria) and CIBSE Knowledge Series KS18 / TM57 principles for IT equipment rooms, with TM52 for assessing the adjacent office overheating/discomfort. The fundamental issue is mixing comfort cooling logic with critical IT cooling in a non-purpose-designed space. Primary cause for the office complaints: the wall-mounted split is oversized for steady-state load but undersized for peak, short-cycling and dumping cold air through the partition (poor insulation, cable penetrations, door undercuts) into the adjacent office, creating local overcooling and draught at the partition (operative temperature <20°C, air velocity >0.25 m/s). Primary cause for server room instability: a single split unit provides no redundancy (N configuration), no humidity control and inadequate airflow management — there is no hot-aisle/cold-aisle separation, so recirculation around cabinets causes inlet temperature spikes when the split cycles off; ASHRAE TC9.9 recommends 18–27°C at server inlet, and the 15–28°C swing violates this. Secondary causes: no leak detection or condensate management appropriate for a critical space; partition wall not acoustically or thermally rated for the duty; the office FCU system has no awareness of the additional sensible load conducted through the partition. Recommended: (1) measure server inlet temperatures (per ASHRAE TC9.9), partition surface temperature, and office-side air velocity and operative temperature; (2) log the split DX cycling and the server room temperature trace over a week; (3) relocate the IT load to a purpose-built comms room or colocation, or, if retention is essential, install N+1 close-control units (CRAC/CRAH) with hot-aisle containment, sized for full IT load plus envelope gains; (4) seal and insulate the partition, door and all service penetrations; (5) raise the server room setpoint to 24°C (within ASHRAE recommended envelope) to reduce conducted overcooling of the adjacent office; (6) review office FCU control to compensate for residual partition gain/loss.
answer.citation: CIBSE Guide A (2015), Section 1; CIBSE TM52 (2013); CIBSE KS18 / TM57 (Integrated School Design — IT rooms guidance is analogous); ASHRAE TC9.9 Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments
